title: Your rule, finished for now
hook: a rule is never finished; this one is ready: Rikyu shakes leaves onto a swept path, and the Talmud leaves a wall bare
tomorrow: even settled at home, what does the Torah call you?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the one-breath rule. The whole thing on one foot, for the hard days. Today the long version gets copied out clean, and called ready.

Every app on your phone has a version number, and none of them is the last one. Japan's tea masters had their own way of living with that. In The Book of Tea, written in English by Okakura Kakuzo, the tea master Sen no Rikyu watches his son sweep and water the garden path. Not clean enough, he says. The son sweeps again, for a weary hour, until there's nothing left to do. Then Rikyu steps into the garden and shakes a tree.
screen: `NO VERSION IS THE LAST.` → `NOT CLEAN ENOUGH.` → `RIKYU SHAKES A TREE.`

segments.voice: Gold and crimson leaves scatter over the clean path. Okakura explains: what Rikyu wanted was "not cleanliness alone, but the beautiful and the natural also." Okakura calls this outlook Teaism, a worship of the imperfect: a tea room left a little bare, a bowl a little uneven, room left for life to finish it. So, today's question: when is a rule finished? The tea way's answer is: when it's ready, not when it's perfect. A swept path with a few leaves on it is ready for guests. Now a neighbor, in its own words. In the Talmud, after the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed, the sages taught that a person may plaster their house but leave a small part bare, a cubit by a cubit, in memory of Jerusalem. Some Jewish homes still keep the custom, a bare patch of wall opposite the door. What's shared: both leave a house unfinished on purpose. The honest difference: Rikyu's leaves delight in things as they are; the bare patch mourns what was lost and waits for Jerusalem to be rebuilt. One smiles at imperfection. The other promises not to forget. A rule can be ready for guests and still waiting.
screen: `NOT CLEANLINESS ALONE.` · `TEAISM: A WORSHIP OF THE IMPERFECT.` · `A CUBIT LEFT BARE FOR JERUSALEM.` · `ONE DELIGHTS; ONE REMEMBERS.` · then, large: `READY, NOT PERFECT.`

segments.voice: On a clean page, copy out draft two slowly, in your best handwriting. If a letter comes out crooked, leave it there, a leaf on the path. When you reach the end, read the top line once and set the pen down.
Your rule: the practice you've built, written out clean and called ready. Ready, not perfect, like a swept path with a few leaves.
Hold onto this: ready for now, leaves and all. Day seventeen hundred, and the rule is written.

screen: `DAY 1700 COUNTS.` → `YOUR RULE · 12 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: EVEN SETTLED AT HOME, WHAT DOES THE TORAH CALL YOU?`

howItsDone: In the way of tea, a room or garden is left a little imperfect on purpose; in Jewish law, a small patch of a home is left unplastered in memory of Jerusalem. On a personal rule, the finished draft is copied out by hand and treated as ready for now, open to later revision.
